import Mathlib.Probability.Kernel.WithDensity
import Mathlib.Probability.Kernel.Invariance
import Mathlib.Data.ENNReal.BigOperators

open MeasureTheory ProbabilityTheory
open scoped ENNReal NNReal

variable {ι α β : Type*} [Fintype ι] [MeasurableSpace α] [MeasurableSpace β]

noncomputable def finiteMixture (w : ι → ℝ≥0) (κ : ι → Kernel α β)
    [∀ i, IsSFiniteKernel (κ i)] : Kernel α β :=
  ∑ i, (κ i).withDensity (fun _ _ => (w i : ℝ≥0∞))

private theorem finiteMixture_apply (w : ι → ℝ≥0) (κ : ι → Kernel α β)
    [∀ i, IsSFiniteKernel (κ i)] (a : α) :
    finiteMixture w κ a = ∑ i, (w i : ℝ≥0∞) • κ i a := by
  classical
  rw [finiteMixture, sum_apply]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro i _
  rw [Kernel.withDensity_apply _ measurable_const, MeasureTheory.withDensity_const]

example (w : ι → ℝ≥0) (κ : ι → Kernel α α)
    [∀ i, IsSFiniteKernel (κ i)] (μ : Measure α)
    (hsum : ∑ i, w i = 1) (hκ : ∀ i, (κ i).Invariant μ) :
    (finiteMixture w κ).Invariant μ := by
  have hsum' : ∑ i, (w i : ℝ≥0∞) = 1 := by
    simpa using congrArg (fun r : ℝ≥0 => (r : ℝ≥0∞)) hsum
  change μ.bind (finiteMixture w κ) = μ
  ext s hs
  calc
    (μ.bind (finiteMixture w κ)) s = ∫⁻ a, ∑ i, (w i : ℝ≥0∞) * κ i a s ∂μ := by
      rw [Measure.bind_apply hs (Kernel.aemeasurable _)]
      simp only [finiteMixture_apply, Measure.finsetSum_apply, Measure.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul]
    _ = ∑ i, ∫⁻ a, (w i : ℝ≥0∞) * κ i a s ∂μ :=
      lintegral_finsetSum _ (fun i _ => ((κ i).measurable_coe hs).const_mul _)
    _ = ∑ i, (w i : ℝ≥0∞) * μ s := by
      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
      intro i _
      rw [lintegral_const_mul _ ((κ i).measurable_coe hs),
        ← Measure.bind_apply hs (κ i).aemeasurable, (hκ i).def]
    _ = μ s := by rw [← Finset.sum_mul, hsum', one_mul]

The tracked ActualAugmentedKernelInvariance module uses this invariant-mixture lemma in its conditional mixture proof; RandomScanHeatBath uses the same pointwise mixture evaluation. This is an audit of a generic reusable argument, not a quotation or formalization claim about the full PBPS algorithm. Only project-original and Mathlib API material is used.
steps: Fix a measurable output event T. Each map \(x\mapsto K_i(x,T)\) is measurable. A fixed w_i is a measurable constant density, so the value of the scaled kernel on T is exactly \(w_i K_i(x,T)\); the definition is not using the nonmeasurable-density fallback. The finite sum is a kernel with measurable event evaluations.

Use the definition of the composed measure and finite additivity of the nonnegative integral for measurable summands. Since each coefficient is constant in x, \[\begin{aligned}(\mu K_w)(T)&=\int_X\sum_i w_iK_i(x,T)\,d\mu(x)\\&=\sum_i w_i\int_X K_i(x,T)\,d\mu(x).\end{aligned}\] These are extended nonnegative quantities, not differences of potentially infinite numbers. No integrability as a finite real number is needed.

Use \(\mu K_i=\mu\) in each integral. The result is \(\sum_i w_i\mu(T)=(\sum_i w_i)\mu(T)=\mu(T)\). Distributivity is in the extended nonnegative reals, where a zero weight contributes zero even for infinite event mass. The conclusion holds on all measurable T, hence as a measure equality.

On \(X=\{0,1\}\) with its discrete measurable structure, take the identity kernel I and the deterministic flip F, both of which preserve the uniform probability π. Give I weight \(3/4\) at 0 and \(1/4\) at 1; give F the complementary weights. Both rows then put mass \(3/4\) at 0 and \(1/4\) at 1. This is still a Markov kernel, but \((\pi K)(\{0\})=3/4\ne 1/2=\pi(\{0\})\). The factors now depend on the input integrated against π, so they cannot in general be pulled outside the integrals.
